strengths: The paper addresses a timely, practically important question—security of agentic 'vibe coding'—and constructs a genuinely novel benchmark (SUSVIBES) that is repository-level, multi-file, and agent-oriented, addressing clear gaps in prior single-file/single-turn security benchmarks (Table 1 comparison is convincing).

The automatic curation pipeline (mining vulnerability-fix commits, masking the feature with LLM-guided deletion, generating task descriptions, and adaptively verifying via line-by-line justification) is thoughtfully designed to avoid leakage of the fix into the task and to ensure the generated request is both necessary and sufficient for reproducing the canonical secure implementation. The verification loop (Figure 4) is a good methodological safeguard against a common failure mode (mismatched or under-specified synthetic tasks).

The scale and diversity of the benchmark (200 tasks, 77 CWEs, 108 repos, 10 domains, 172 lines edited on average) substantially exceeds prior repository-level security benchmarks (ASE, SecureAgentBench), and the fully automated environment-building (Dockerization) pipeline is a nontrivial engineering contribution that improves reproducibility/scalability.

The experiments span 3 agent frameworks x 3 backbone LLMs (9 combinations) plus a Gemini 3 Pro follow-up, giving reasonably broad coverage of current frontier systems, and the central finding—high functional pass rates but very low secure pass rates (~10%)—is a striking, well-supported, and important result for the community.

The mitigation study (generic/self-selection/oracle CWE hints) is a nice negative result showing naive prompting does not reliably help, and the transition-matrix analysis (Figure 8) offering a mechanistic explanation (security focus trades off against functional coverage) adds useful nuance beyond a simple summary statistic.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix D) with concrete CWE-level explanations (CRLF injection, XSS via javascript: scheme, session-expiry bypass) ground the aggregate statistics in interpretable, real vulnerabilities, improving the credibility and narrative clarity of the security claims.
weaknesses: Reliance on unit tests (both functional and 'security') as the sole ground truth for security correctness is a significant soundness concern: passing a small number of security tests (mean 3.7 per task) does not guarantee the absence of other vulnerabilities, and failing them does not necessarily mean the code is meaningfully less secure than the reference—the paper acknowledges this only briefly in Appendix E rather than in the main text where the strong claims are made.

The entire pipeline (mask generation, task description generation, mask verification, environment building, Docker image construction) relies heavily on LLM agents (SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet) without independent human verification at scale; only high-level automated verification loops are described, raising concerns about pipeline-induced biases, artifacts, or label noise that could affect the reported benchmark difficulty and security statistics but are not quantified (e.g., no human audit of a sample of the 200 final tasks/tests reported).

The task construction process explicitly avoids mentioning security in the generated task description ('Do NOT mention security-related considerations'), which is reasonable for the main results, but this means the entire framing of 'agents fail at security' partly reflects that agents were never told security was a concern in most settings—the paper does distinguish generic vs. oracle settings, but the core headline numbers (e.g., 10.5% SECPASS) still include the generic security reminder, and the more informative 'no reminder at all' condition is not reported, making it hard to disentangle 'agents don't know to think about security' from 'agents can't produce secure code even when told to'.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as single pass@1 percentages over 200 tasks without confidence intervals, variance across repeated runs, or significance testing, despite LLM agent outputs being stochastic; this makes some comparisons (e.g., small percentage-point differences between frameworks in Table 6, or the CWE overlap percentages in Figure 6) difficult to interpret rigorously.

The mitigation section's core explanatory hypothesis (agents trade off functionality for security under prompting) is plausible but supported mainly by one illustrative anecdote (the wagtail step-count example) and a single transition matrix for one model/framework combination, rather than a broader controlled study; the generality of this trade-off across models/frameworks is asserted but not fully demonstrated.

The benchmark and experiments are restricted entirely to Python, which is explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but nonetheless limits the generality of claims about 'vibe coding' broadly, since many production vibe-coding contexts involve JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, or other languages with different vulnerability profiles.

Cost/compute details (number of LLM calls, total tokens/dollars spent constructing the benchmark and running the 9+ agent-model evaluations) are not reported, which would help assess reproducibility and practical accessibility of the benchmark for other researchers with more limited budgets.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important question—whether agentic 'vibe coding' produces secure code—with a much more realistic evaluation setting (full repositories, multi-turn agents, execution feedback) than prior single-file/single-turn security benchmarks.

The automatic curation pipeline (mining real vulnerability-fix commits, reverting to pre-fix state, harnessing human-written functional and security tests, and using an LLM-driven mask/verify loop) is a reasonably clever and scalable way to generate large numbers of grounded, historically-verified tasks without manual annotation of every instance.

Broad coverage relative to related work: 200 repository-level tasks spanning 77 CWEs and 108 projects across 10 domains, with substantially larger average edit size than comparable benchmarks (Table 1), which is a genuine scale/coverage advantage.

The experiments are reasonably comprehensive (3 agent frameworks x 3 backbone LLMs, plus Gemini 3 Pro follow-up, plus three prompting-based mitigation strategies), and the core finding—large functionality/security gap, and mitigation prompts trading off functionality for marginal security gains—is a clear, actionable, and somewhat counter-intuitive result.

The qualitative case studies (timing side-channel in Django-like password verification, CRLF/header injection, javascript: URL XSS, session max_age bypass) are concrete and illustrate real, non-trivial vulnerability classes that pure functional testing would miss, lending some credibility to the security test suite design.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM agents (SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet) not only to generate but also to verify the benchmark tasks (masking, description writing, line-by-line verification) raises circularity and construct-validity concerns: since one of the exact model/agent combinations used for curation is later evaluated on the resulting benchmark, it is unclear whether reported functionality/security numbers reflect genuine agent capability or artifacts of the curation model's own blind spots/preferences (e.g., systematically easier or harder tasks for Claude-based agents). No human study or independent model is used to validate task quality, description fidelity, or absence of leakage from the fix into the task description.

The security evaluation is entirely test-based (avg. only 3.7 security tests per task, sometimes far fewer), so it can only catch the specific vulnerability class the original human fix addressed; it cannot detect other vulnerabilities the agent's alternative-but-different implementation might introduce, nor can it credit agents whose secure implementation diverges from the canonical patch but still passes tests only partially. This risks both false negatives (missed vulnerabilities) and unfair penalization of functionally/semantically valid alternative implementations that fail the narrowly scoped security test.

Results are reported as single-run pass@1 with no repeated sampling, variance estimates, or confidence intervals, despite agent behavior being known to be highly stochastic across runs (especially with 200-step interactive rollouts); this weakens the statistical reliability of fine-grained comparisons such as the CWE-level 'cautious CWE' breakdown (Figure 6) or the small-sample repository-level Table 4 (as few as a handful of tasks per repo/CWE cell).

The mitigation-strategy analysis (Section 5) is conducted only on a single agent/model pairing (SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet), yet the paper generalizes the conclusion ('preliminary strategies cannot mitigate security issues') to vibe coding broadly; this is a substantial overreach given the demonstrated CWE- and agent-specific heterogeneity shown elsewhere in the same paper (Figure 6, Table 4).

Automated components critical to correctness of the reported metrics—LLM-synthesized regex log parsers (Appendix A.3.2) and LLM-built Docker environments (Appendix A.3.1)—are themselves unvalidated by humans at scale; errors in parsing test outputs or environment construction could silently mislabel FuncPass/SecPass outcomes, and no inter-rater or manual audit of a sample of environments/parsers is reported.

The benchmark is restricted to Python only, and the paper's broader claims about 'vibe coding' safety in general are not tempered enough given this single-language, single-paradigm (feature-request) scope; other common vibe-coding scenarios (bug fixes, refactors, greenfield generation) are not covered.

Presentation issues: Table 4's column semantics ('FuncPass & SecPass⊥FuncPass') are not clearly explained in-line and are hard to parse; Figure 8/9's transition-matrix and trend-quantification methodology is described tersely and would benefit from a worked numeric example; some claims (e.g., '58% CWEs are not overlapped') lack precise definition of the denominator.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: existing secure-code benchmarks are single-file/single-turn, while this work targets repository-level, multi-turn agentic coding, which is much closer to real 'vibe coding' usage.

The automatic curation pipeline (mine vulnerability-fix commits → revert → mask feature → generate task description → adaptively verify mask against canonical secure implementation) is a genuinely clever and largely scalable design that could be extended to new languages/vulnerabilities.

Table 1 shows SUSVIBES substantially exceeds prior benchmarks in scale of context, number of edited lines, and CWE diversity (77 CWEs vs. <45 in comparable benchmarks), giving it broad and realistic coverage.

Comprehensive experimental matrix (3 agent frameworks × 3 backbone LLMs, plus a Gemini 3 Pro follow-up) yields a consistent and striking finding: high functional pass rates (up to 61%) co-occur with very low security pass rates (~10%), a disturbing and well-supported headline result.

The security-mitigation experiments (generic/self-selection/oracle prompting) are a valuable negative result, showing that naive prompting-based fixes actually trade off functionality for security rather than solving the problem, and the transition-matrix analysis (Fig. 8) nicely dissects this trade-off.

Qualitative case studies (timing side-channel in Django, CRLF injection in buildbot, XSS in wagtail, session-expiry bypass in aiohttp_session) are concrete, technically convincing, and illustrate genuinely subtle vulnerabilities that would be easy for a human reviewer to miss, strengthening the paper's real-world relevance.

The appendix is unusually thorough (prompts, Docker-environment construction process, CWE statistics, limitations), aiding reproducibility and transparency about design choices, including explicit discussion of risks introduced by giving agents Docker access during curation.
weaknesses: Security evaluation relies entirely on human-written Tsecure unit tests harvested from the original fix commit (mean of only 3.7 tests per task); these tests target the one historically known CWE and may not detect other/new vulnerabilities the agent could introduce elsewhere in its patch, so 'SecPass' likely overstates security compared to a true audit.

Multiple curation stages (mask generation, task description generation, mask verification) rely on LLM judgment (SWE-Agent/Claude) rather than human validation at scale; despite the adaptive verification loop, there is limited quantitative evidence (e.g., human-audited sample, agreement rate) on how often masks are still too permissive/restrictive or leak fix information.

Results are reported as single pass@1 numbers without confidence intervals or repeated-sampling variance, despite LLM agents being stochastic and some CWE-stratified subsets (Fig. 6, Table 4) being very small (single-digit task counts per category), which weakens the statistical reliability of fine-grained claims (e.g., 'different models favor different CWEs').

The benchmark is Python-only and drawn from a specific set of GitHub domains, which the authors acknowledge, but this still constrains how strongly the 'vibe coding is unsafe' conclusion generalizes across languages/ecosystems.

The 'preliminary mitigation' strategies tested (generic reminder, self-selection, oracle CWE) are all simple prompting variants; the negative results, while informative, are somewhat expected and the paper does not explore more structured mitigations (e.g., static analysis tool integration, multi-agent review) that would better test whether the security gap is fundamentally addressable.

Environment construction itself is agent-generated (Docker images built by an SWE-Agent instance), which the paper admits carries its own risks and potential inconsistencies; the extent of manual QA on the resulting 200 execution environments is not fully quantified.

strengths: Addresses a timely, practically important question (security of vibe-coding agent output) with a novel repository-level benchmark grounded in real, historically-fixed vulnerabilities rather than synthetic injections, which increases ecological validity.

The curation pipeline is thoughtfully engineered: it separates functional vs. security tests from vulnerability-fix commits, uses an adaptive masking/verification loop to ensure the task description neither leaks the fix nor omits required functionality, and includes execution-based validation across {C0, C-1, C-1^M} x {Tfunc, Tfunc+Tsecure} combinations plus a human expert pass to decouple security tests from the reference implementation.

Broad and rigorous evaluation: 12 agent-framework/LLM combinations across 186 tasks spanning 79 CWE types and 10 application domains, substantially larger CWE and context coverage than prior benchmarks (Table 1), with clear comparison to related work.

The core finding -- high FuncPass but very low SecPass, and that security remains poor even when the agent is given the oracle CWE type -- is a striking, well-supported, and actionable result with clear practical implications for vibe-coding adoption.

Rich supplementary analyses (per-CWE breakdown, domain-stratified comparisons, task-complexity vs. performance, CWE self-identification precision/recall) and detailed, illustrative case studies (e.g., timing side-channel in Django, CRLF injection in Buildbot, XSS in Wagtail, session-expiry bypass in aiohttp-session) that make the security risks concrete and convincing.
Reasonably transparent methodology with extensive appendix documentation of prompts and pipeline stages, aiding reproducibility, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: Security evaluation relies entirely on a small number of dynamic tests (mean 3.5 Tsecure tests per task); despite human verification, this leaves open the possibility that some 'secure' solutions merely dodge the specific tested exploit rather than the underlying vulnerability class, and that some genuinely insecure-but-untested variants are misclassified as secure.

Results are reported as single-run pass@1 without repeated sampling or variance estimates, despite agent stochasticity; combined with fine-grained CWE-category or domain-stratified breakdowns (Table 4, Figure 4) computed on very small subgroup sample sizes, many reported differences may not be statistically robust.

The benchmark construction pipeline itself heavily relies on LLM agents (SWE-Agent, Claude, o3) for masking, task-description generation, verification, and environment/log-parser synthesis; aside from the final security-test quality check by 5 experts (whose inter-annotator agreement is not reported), there is little independent human validation of overall task realism, difficulty calibration, or potential artifacts introduced by this LLM-in-the-loop curation.

The mitigation study (Section 5) is fairly narrow -- only two simple prompting strategies tested on a single agent/model combination (SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet) -- which limits how strongly the paper's broader claim that 'preliminary security strategies cannot mitigate these issues' generalizes across frameworks and models.
The abstract contains apparently unfinished/placeholder text (dangling sentences about code/dataset availability and leaderboard), suggesting incomplete proofreading of the submission.

Limited discussion of environment reproducibility/maintenance risk (e.g., whether the ~200 Docker-based execution environments built via LLM automation remain stable and non-flaky over time as upstream dependencies evolve), and no reported measure of test flakiness across repeated runs.

strengths: Addresses a highly timely and practically important question (security of AI-agent-generated code in realistic 'vibe coding' settings) that is underexplored relative to functionality-focused benchmarks like SWE-bench.

The automatic curation pipeline is sophisticated and well-engineered: it mines real historical vulnerability-fix commits, uses an adaptive masking/verification loop to ensure task descriptions cover the canonical secure implementation without leaking security hints, and validates functional/security test behavior across {C0, C-1, C^M-1} x {Tfunc, Tsecure} combinations.

Benchmark scale and realism exceed prior work along several axes (79 CWE types, repository-level context with ~236K LOC on average, multi-file target patches with ~175 edited lines), as summarized clearly in the comparison table against CWEval, SALLM, SecCodePLT, Asleep, BaxBench, and SecureAgentBench.

Comprehensive experimental matrix (3 agent frameworks x 4 frontier LLMs = 12 settings) with a clean, interpretable metric design (FuncPass, SecPass, SecPass⊥FuncPass) that disentangles functional and security capability.

Thorough qualitative case studies (timing side-channel in Django, CRLF/header injection in Buildbot, stored XSS in Wagtail, session-expiration bypass in aiohttp-session) that convincingly ground the quantitative findings in concrete, exploitable vulnerabilities.

Includes a human verification/augmentation phase for security test quality (5 experts, rubric-based review) to reduce false negatives from tests overly coupled to the reference implementation, and reports the resulting decoupling statistics.
Provides a reasonably candid limitations section and useful appendix analyses (task complexity vs. performance, CWE coverage breakdown, curation yield statistics).
weaknesses: Benchmark size (186 tasks) is small for the granularity of some reported breakdowns (e.g., Table 4's per-domain SecPass⊥FuncPass figures such as 0.0%/33.3%/50.0% strongly suggest very small per-cell task counts), undermining the statistical reliability of several domain- and CWE-stratified claims.

The entire curation pipeline (masking, task description generation, description-to-implementation verification, environment construction, log-parser synthesis) is itself LLM-driven (mostly SWE-Agent/Claude and o3), with human verification applied only to security test quality, not to the fidelity/realism of generated task descriptions or masks; this creates a risk that pipeline artifacts (over/under-specification, subtle information leakage, or unnatural phrasing) systematically bias the measured FuncPass/SecPass rates in ways not fully controlled for.

Preliminary mitigation experiments (self-selection, oracle CWE hints) are conducted only on a single framework/model combination (SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet), which limits how much can be concluded about mitigation strategies' generality across the broader 12-setting evaluation matrix used for the main results.

Only pass@1 is reported with no repeated sampling or variance/significance analysis, despite known run-to-run stochasticity in agentic systems and small task counts, making some cross-model/cross-framework rankings (e.g., Gemini 3 Pro vs. Gemini 2.5 Pro security comparisons) less robust than presented.

Benchmark is restricted to Python repositories, and the environment-construction/execution pipeline (also agent-built Docker images) raises reproducibility questions about whether all 186 environments are stable, deterministic, and free of the "operational risks" the authors themselves note (e.g., permissive network exposure, uncleaned artifacts) during construction.

The paper does not report a human/expert baseline or any sensitivity analysis of how strict security tests are (e.g., rate of legitimate alternative secure implementations still failing tests despite the human review, beyond the ~44% "conditional pass" figure mentioned only for test coverage, not for final scored results).

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important question—the security of AI-agent-generated code in realistic 'vibe coding' settings—that is underexplored relative to the heavy focus on functional correctness in prior SWE-agent benchmarks.

The automatic curation pipeline is carefully engineered with multiple verification stages (adaptive line-by-line linking of the canonical secure implementation to the generated task description, execution-based validation across {C0, C-1, C_masked} x {func, func+security} test combinations, and a 5-expert human verification pass on security tests), which meaningfully increases confidence in task validity and reduces implementation-coupling of the security tests.

Substantial scale and diversity relative to existing secure-code-generation benchmarks (Table 1): repository-level context, 79 CWE types, larger average patch size (175 lines) and multi-file edits, spanning 10 real-world application domains from 100 repositories.

Comprehensive experimental matrix (3 frameworks x 4 backbone models = 12 settings) with a clean, informative decomposition of results (FuncPass vs SecPass vs SecPass⊥FuncPass) that isolates model/framework capability from underlying task difficulty.

The findings are striking and clearly presented (e.g., 79.3% of functionally correct SWE-Agent+Claude solutions are insecure), and the CWE-category and domain-stratified analyses (Fig. 4, Table 4) add nuance by showing complementary strengths across models/frameworks rather than a single dominant system.

The mitigation experiments (self-selection, oracle CWE hints) are a valuable negative result showing that naive prompting strategies trade off functional correctness for marginal security gains, with a thoughtful transition-matrix analysis (Fig. 5) explaining the mechanism behind the limited gains.

Strong transparency/reproducibility effort: full prompts for mask generation, task description generation, verification, environment construction, and mitigation strategies are provided in the appendix, along with detailed curation yield statistics (Table 10) and qualitative case studies with full patch diffs.
Honest limitations section acknowledging Python-only scope and reliance on test outcomes as a security proxy, with concrete future directions.
weaknesses: Task/CWE granularity is thin: with 186 tasks and 79 CWE types (91.9% single-labeled), several stratified breakdowns (e.g., Table 4's per-domain, per-CWE-category comparison) likely rest on very small per-cell sample sizes, making some conclusions (e.g., 'security winner varies by domain') statistically fragile despite being stated fairly assertively.

Heavy reliance on LLM agents (SWE-Agent instances) for multiple pipeline stages—mask generation, task description writing, and description-to-implementation verification—introduces a chain of potential systematic biases or errors that are only partially checked by human verification (which is applied specifically to security test quality, not to task description fidelity/leakage or mask correctness at scale).

Results are reported as pass@1 with no repeated sampling or variance analysis, so it is unclear how much of the observed differences between models/frameworks (some quite small, e.g., SecPass differences of a few points) reflect genuine capability gaps versus run-to-run stochasticity.

The benchmark is restricted to Python repositories, and construction depends on the availability of well-documented CI/CD pipelines and dockerizable test suites, which may bias the selected repositories toward more mature/well-maintained projects and not fully represent the 'vibe coding' long tail of smaller or less rigorously tested codebases.

The curation pipeline is computationally and engineering-intensive (multiple agent rollouts per task for masking/description/verification, plus Docker environment synthesis with agent-driven Dockerfile creation and test-log-parser synthesis via a separate LLM), which may limit independent reproducibility or extension by other groups without similar infrastructure and API budgets.

The mitigation strategies explored are intentionally shallow (single-turn prompting variants), so the paper's claim that 'more rigorous training and structured planning protocols' are needed is plausible but not empirically substantiated by any stronger intervention (e.g., multi-turn security review, tool-augmented static analysis) within the paper itself.
